lead: Measuring a Turing machine's cost turns 'this machine is fast' into a function of input length n. Time counts steps; space counts tape cells. The worst case over all inputs of length n is the standard measure. These functions sort languages into classes TIME(t(n)) and SPACE(s(n)). The idea compares algorithms independently of machine details and leads to P and NP. Only a few universities teach this chapter in detail.
prereq: You need Unit 5 for tapes, heads and configurations, and 6.2 for decidable problems.

blocks.text: Let M halt on every input. For input w, n = |w|. The running time on w is the number of steps before M halts. The running time t(n) is the maximum of these counts over all inputs of length n. The space used on w is the number of distinct tape cells scanned. The space s(n) is the maximum over all inputs of length n. Both are worst-case: one slow input of length n sets t(n).

Big-O and Θ describe growth. f(n) = O(g(n)) when constants c > 0 and n₀ exist with f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀. f(n) = Θ(g(n)) when f = O(g) and g = O(f). For example, 3n² + 5n = Θ(n²). Constants drop out, so machine details do not change the class.
TIME(t(n)) = { L | some TM decides L in time O(t(n)) }
blocks.where: L is a language; t(n) is a time bound; the machine halts on every input.

blocks.text: SPACE(s(n)) = { L | some TM decides L using O(s(n)) work cells }
blocks.where: s(n) is a space bound; on a read-only input tape only work cells count.

blocks.text: On a single-tape machine the input sits on the work tape. Reading the input scans cells, so a machine using n input cells has space at least n. Many theorems want to discuss space below n. The standard fix is a read-only input tape plus work tapes. The input head reads but cannot write. Space counts only work-tape cells. A machine can then use log₂ n space while reading all n input symbols.

items: A machine running in time t(n), with t(n) ≥ n, scans at most t(n) + 1 cells: one new cell per step plus the starting cell.
TIME(f(n)) ⊆ SPACE(f(n)) for f(n) ≥ n, because each step visits at most one new cell.
SPACE(s(n)) ⊆ TIME(2^(O(s(n)))) for s(n) ≥ log₂ n, because the number of configurations is bounded by 2^(O(s)).

blocks.text: The time and space hierarchy theorems say that with more time or space, strictly more languages are decidable, for reasonable constructible bounds. A machine that diagonalises against all smaller-bound machines proves this. We quote the result. P, NP and completeness are in 6.8.

spec.aria: Two bars on one step axis from 0 to 36: M₁ is 7 steps long; M₂ is three rounds of 12 steps, ending at 36.

examples.question: The word w = 000111 has length n = 6. Machine M₁ scans to the end and checks that the last two symbols are 1s. Machine M₂ decides {0ᵏ1ᵏ} by crossing out one 0 and one 1 per round. Compare their time and space on w. Give the worst-case time class of each.
steps: n = |w| = 6, so k = 3 zeros and 3 ones.
M₁ reads n symbols and makes one final check: n + 1 = 6 + 1 = 7 steps. Thus M₁ runs in TIME(n).
M₂ does k = 3 rounds. Each round crosses one 0 and one 1 and scans at most 2n = 12 cells.
Total steps at most k × 2n = 3 × 12 = 36 = n². Thus M₂ runs in TIME(n²).
M₂ writes only on the n input cells, so it uses at most n = 6 cells. On a single tape, space is at least n.
examples.answer: M₁ uses 7 steps; M₂ uses at most 36 steps (3 rounds of at most 12 cells); both use 6 cells, so M₁ is in TIME(n) and M₂ in TIME(n²).

n = 6
m1 = n + 1
k = n // 2
scan = 2 * n
m2 = k * scan
space = n
print(m1)

print(m2)
print(space)

traps: Measuring time against the value written in the input, not its length. A number near 2ⁿ written in binary has length only n.
Forgetting that on a single tape the input cells count as space, so space is at least n.
Calling O(n) and Θ(n) the same. O is an upper bound; Θ is a tight bound.
Ignoring the worst case: t(n) is set by the slowest input of length n.
Using a read-only input tape and then counting input cells as space; in that model only work cells count.

quiz.q: Define t(n) and s(n) for a Turing machine M.
quiz.a: t(n) is the maximum number of steps of M over all inputs of length n. s(n) is the maximum number of distinct tape cells scanned over all inputs of length n.

quiz.q: Why is space at least n on a single-tape machine?
quiz.a: The input is stored on the same tape as the work. Reading n input symbols already scans n cells, so the space count cannot be below n.

quiz.q: A machine makes n² + 3n steps. Give its Θ class and a TIME class.
quiz.a: Θ(n²), because the n² term dominates. It lies in TIME(n²).

quiz.q: A machine runs in time t(n) = n³ with t(n) ≥ n. Bound its space on a single tape.
quiz.a: It uses at most t(n) + 1 = n³ + 1 cells, so it lies in SPACE(n³).

quiz.q: Why does SPACE(s) ⊆ TIME(2^(O(s))) need s(n) ≥ log₂ n?
quiz.a: The number of configurations includes input head positions. The bound 2^(O(s)) covers n positions only when n ≤ 2^(O(s)), which holds when s(n) ≥ log₂ n.

quiz.q: A language is in TIME(n²). Is it also in SPACE(n²)? Justify.
quiz.a: Yes. Here f(n) = n² ≥ n, and TIME(f) ⊆ SPACE(f), so the language is in SPACE(n²).

beyond: Not for the exam. Complexity classes lead to P versus NP, circuit lower bounds and fine-grained complexity. Researchers also study space-bounded classes such as L and PSPACE, and quantum time classes such as BQP. Search next for 'time hierarchy theorem', 'space hierarchy theorem' and 'Savitch's theorem'.
